title: NeuroMuscle Lab
text:
What we study
We are neurologists and researchers studying ALS, SBMA and related neuromuscular diseases. We combine patient cohorts and clinical trials with RNA biology, genetics and reproducible, large-scale data analysis.

title: NeuroMuscle Lab
text:
The lab
Our lab is in the Campus Biomedico Pietro d’Abano, Via Orus 2B, Padova. Our patients are seen at the Motor Neuron Disease Centre of Azienda Ospedale Università Padova, where we also run clinical trials. Explore the lab · Clinical trials

title: Privacy policy
text:
Types of Data collected
Among the types of Personal Data that this Application collects, by itself or through third parties, there are: first name; last name; email address; phone number (optional); link to a curriculum vitae; Usage Data.
Complete details on each type of Personal Data collected are given in the dedicated sections of this privacy policy or in specific explanation texts displayed before the Data are collected. Personal Data may be freely provided by the User or, in the case of Usage Data, collected automatically when using this Application.
Unless specified otherwise, all Data requested by this Application are mandatory, and failure to provide them may make it impossible for this Application to provide its Service. Where this Application states that some Data are not mandatory, such as the phone number in the application form, Users are free not to communicate them without consequences for the availability or functioning of the Service.
Users who are uncertain about which Personal Data are mandatory are welcome to contact the Owner. Any use of Cookies or other tracking tools by this Application or by third-party services it uses serves to provide the Service required by the User, in addition to any other purposes described in this document and in the Cookie Policy.
Users are responsible for any third-party Personal Data obtained, published or shared through this Application.

title: Privacy policy
section: Mode and place of processing the Data
text:
Mode and place of processing the Data

Methods of processing
The Owner takes appropriate security measures to prevent unauthorised access, disclosure, modification or unauthorised destruction of the Data. Processing is carried out using computers and IT-enabled tools, following organisational procedures and methods strictly related to the purposes indicated. In addition to the Owner, the Data may in some cases be accessible to certain types of persons in charge, involved with the operation of this Application (administration, legal, system administration), or to external parties (such as third-party technical service providers, hosting providers or IT companies) appointed, if necessary, as Data Processors by the Owner. The updated list of these parties may be requested from the Owner at any time.


Place
The Data are processed at the Owner’s operating offices and in any other places where the parties involved in the processing are located. Depending on the User’s location, data transfers may involve transferring the User’s Data to a country other than their own. To find out more about the place of processing of such transferred Data, Users can check the section containing details about the processing of Personal Data.


Retention time
Unless specified otherwise in this document, Personal Data shall be processed and stored for as long as required by the purpose they have been collected for, and may be retained for longer due to an applicable legal obligation or based on the Users’ consent.

title: Privacy policy
text:

title: How fatigability progresses in SBMA
text:
Fatigue is one of the most disabling symptoms of spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA), but fatigability, the drop in performance during sustained activity, had never been followed over time.
In a retrospective study of 168 people with SBMA (703 visits), we measured fatigability as the decline in distance walked between the first and the sixth minute of the six-minute walk test. Almost half of the patients were fatigable at baseline, and fatigability was linked to lower-limb and trunk function and to walking distance.
Paper: Zanovello M, Sabbatini D, Paredi F, et al. Longitudinal progression of 6-minute walk test-derived fatigability in spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy: a retrospective study. Muscle & Nerve, 2026. doi:10.1002/mus.70457

title: Skeletal Muscle in ALS: an international conference in Padova
text:
Skeletal Muscle in ALS: Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Therapeutic Perspectives brought together clinicians and scientists at Hotel Mantegna, Padova, on 25–26 September 2026.
Four sessions covered muscle pathology, models and omics; muscle and neuromuscular junction physiology in ALS; muscle biomarkers; and therapies that target skeletal muscle. Keynote lectures were given by Marco Sandri (University of Padova, VIMM) and Pietro Fratta (UCL), and selected posters were presented as short talks.
The conference was organised by Gianni Sorarù, Maria Pennuto, Manuela Basso and Matteo Zanovello, sponsored by ASLA, with the patronage of the University of Padova and Azienda Ospedale Università Padova.

title: What counts as a meaningful change in SBMA?
text:
To read the results of a clinical trial, we need to know how much change in a score matters to patients. For spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA) this was not known.
We asked people with SBMA how they felt they had changed between visits and compared their answers with the SBMA Functional Rating Scale, its lower-limb and trunk subscale and the six-minute walk test. The study gives the first patient-anchored estimates of the minimal clinically important difference for these measures, supports the use of the subscale, and offers thresholds for responder definitions and sample-size calculations in future SBMA trials.
Paper: Zanovello M, Sabbatini D, Paredi F, et al. Estimating the minimal clinically important difference of functional outcomes in spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy. Journal of Neurology, 2026. doi:10.1007/s00415-026-14032-4
Back to the home page

title: Correcting UNC13A splicing rescues synapses after TDP-43 loss
text:
Loss of TDP-43 from the nucleus is the hallmark of almost all cases of ALS and of about half of frontotemporal dementia. It causes cryptic splicing in hundreds of RNAs, but whether it affects how neurons talk to each other was unclear.
This study, led by Pietro Fratta’s group at UCL with our contribution, shows that TDP-43 loss leaves neurons structurally intact but breaks down synaptic communication. Correcting one cryptic splicing event, in UNC13A, was enough to rescue it. Splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides corrected UNC13A in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanised mouse model, restoring synaptic vesicle release and network synchrony.
Paper: Keuss MJ, Harley P, Ryadnov E, et al. UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss. Nature, 2026. doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11256-2

title: NeuroMuscle Lab
text:
What we can measure



Clinical cohorts and outcomes
Long-term follow-up of people with ALS and SBMA with standard functional scales, the six-minute walk test and patient-anchored change scores. Answers: how disease progresses, and which change is meaningful for a trial.


Neurophysiology
Electromyography, nerve conduction studies, transcranial magnetic stimulation for cortical excitability and motor evoked potentials. Answers: how much upper and lower motor neuron function is lost.


Brain imaging
MRI, including the motor band sign, and [18F]FDG-PET. Answers: where and how strongly the motor system and its glia are affected.


Fluid biomarkers
Neurofilaments, chitinases, serum p-tau181 and creatinine in blood and CSF, and new ELISA assays developed in the lab. Answers: who progresses faster, and whether a treatment reaches its target.


Muscle pathology
Histology and immunostaining of patient muscle biopsies, including phosphorylated tau and markers of regeneration and innervation. Answers: what happens in muscle, not only in the nerve.


RNA and genomic data
RNA-seq analysis of cryptic splicing and polyadenylation, and repeat expansion and variant analysis in population datasets such as the UK Biobank. Answers: which RNA changes mark TDP-43 loss, and how common disease variants are.
